topic.title: Anaerobic respiration in muscle and yeast
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Usually two or three parts inside a respiration or exercise question rather than a question of its own. March 2026 put the muscle word equation at the end of the breathing-graph question and reports that many candidates wrote carbon dioxide instead of energy; Summer 2023 asked what muscle produces without oxygen and many answered alcohol. Expect the equations at [2] each, a comparison at [2], and the yeast practical at [1]-[2] per part.
mustMemorise: Yeast: glucose → energy + alcohol + carbon dioxide
Both routes use glucose and release energy; neither uses oxygen
Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose than aerobic
Muscle produces no gas; yeast's gas is carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky
The oil layer in the yeast tube keeps air out so the respiration is anaerobic
notOnThisSpec: Oxygen debt as a named process — outcome 1.5.5 asks only for a comparison
The biochemistry of fermentation, and industrial fermenter design
Lactic acid being converted back in the liver

note.title: Anaerobic respiration in muscle and yeast
note.subject: science

mustKnow: Anaerobic releases much less energy per glucose than aerobic
Limewater turns milky with carbon dioxide

notOnThisSpec: Oxygen debt as a named process
Lactic acid converted back in the liver

mustBeAbleTo: Write the muscle equation with energy AND lactic acid as the two products
Write the yeast equation with energy, alcohol and carbon dioxide
Say which product belongs to muscle and which to yeast, without hesitating
Give a similarity and a difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration, naming both sides each time
State that anaerobic respiration releases much less energy from the same glucose
Explain why a sprinting muscle respires anaerobically
Describe the yeast investigation: oil layer, delivery tube, limewater turning milky
Explain the purpose of a boiled-yeast control and a no-glucose control
Turn a bubble rate into a total, and read a table of three tubes
sheet.howExamined: B1, 1 hour: 60 marks at Foundation, 70 at Higher, calculator allowed. Anaerobic respiration rarely gets a whole question; it appears as two or three parts inside a respiration or exercise question — a word equation with one mark per box [2], the products of yeast [2], a similarity and a difference [2], and the yeast practical at [1]-[2] per part. Schemes are point-for-point with tight accept lists: 'lactic acid' not 'lactose', 'milky' not 'cloudy', and a difference that names both sides.
traps: Alcohol given as the product of anaerobic respiration in muscle (Summer 2023 B1 F Q2(c)(ii))
Carbon dioxide written where energy belongs in the muscle equation (March 2026 B1 F Q7)
Putting water or oxygen into an anaerobic equation
Saying anaerobic respiration releases more energy, or the same
Describing a difference from one side only
Calling alcohol the gas that makes dough rise — the gas is carbon dioxide
Writing 'cloudy' instead of 'milky' for the limewater result
Thinking the oil is there for warmth rather than to keep oxygen out
Treating the boiled-yeast tube as a repeat rather than a control

workedExamples.stem:
Compare anaerobic respiration in mammalian muscle with anaerobic respiration in yeast.
Give one similarity and two differences. [3]

steps.working: Similarity: both use glucose and neither uses oxygen.
steps.decision: Start with what the two share. A 'compare and contrast' question always has a mark for the similarity, and it is the one candidates skip when they rush to the differences.

steps.working: Difference 1: muscle produces lactic acid; yeast produces alcohol and carbon dioxide.
steps.decision: Name both sides of the difference. 'Muscle makes lactic acid' on its own describes one organism rather than comparing two, and CCEA's schemes ask for comparisons that mention both.

options: Because a difference needs both things described
Because lactic acid is more important
whyMenu.explain: A comparison mark needs the contrast visible on the page: this one does X, that one does Y.

steps.working: Difference 2: yeast releases carbon dioxide as a gas, so you can collect it; muscle releases no gas at all.
steps.decision: A second difference has to be genuinely different from the first, not the same fact reworded. The gas is a fresh point because it is what the practical depends on.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Similarity: both use glucose and neither needs oxygen. Differences: muscle produces lactic acid whereas yeast produces alcohol and carbon dioxide; and yeast gives off a gas that can be collected, whereas muscle produces no gas.

twin.stem: Give one similarity and one difference between aerobic respiration and anaerobic respiration in muscle.

accepted: both use glucose and release energy; aerobic needs oxygen and releases much more energy, while anaerobic in muscle needs no oxygen and produces lactic acid

items.stem: A sprinter's leg muscles run out of oxygen. What do they produce?
items.skill: Keep the muscle and yeast products apart

options.feedback: Muscle makes lactic acid and nothing else. No gas, no water.
That is yeast. Summer 2023 examiners reported candidates giving alcohol where lactic acid was wanted.
Those are the aerobic products, and this muscle has no oxygen.
Glucose is what goes in, and there is no oxygen. Products come out of the arrow.

items.skill: Remember that energy is a product in every respiration equation

options.feedback: Energy is written as a product in all three respiration equations, because respiration is exothermic.
Muscle makes no carbon dioxide without oxygen. March 2026 examiners reported this exact substitution: carbon dioxide written where energy belonged.
There is no oxygen — that is what anaerobic means.
Water is an aerobic product. The only other product here is energy.

items.stem: How does the energy released by anaerobic respiration compare with aerobic respiration, for the same amount of glucose?

options.feedback: Much less from each glucose molecule, which is why anaerobic respiration cannot keep a muscle going for long.
The other way round. Anaerobic respiration leaves most of the energy still locked in the lactic acid or the alcohol.
If it were the same there would be no advantage in breathing. Aerobic respiration releases far more per glucose.

options.text: No energy is released at all
options.feedback: Energy is released — it is in every one of the equations. There is simply much less of it.

items.stem: Gas from a tube of yeast and glucose is bubbled through limewater and the limewater turns milky. What is the gas?

options.feedback: Milky limewater means carbon dioxide, which is one of yeast's two anaerobic products.
Oxygen relights a glowing splint and does nothing to limewater.
Alcohol is yeast's other product, but it stays in the liquid. The gas bubbling through is carbon dioxide.
Hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint. It is not a product of respiration.

context.setting: The muscle equation printed with two empty boxes

parts.stem:
Complete this word equation for anaerobic respiration in a mammalian muscle.

glucose  →  ______ + ______

scheme.for: energy
scheme.examinerNote: March 2026: many candidates wrote carbon dioxide here instead of energy.

scheme.for: lactic acid

hints: Every respiration equation has energy among the products.
Muscle and yeast make different things — this is the muscle one.

commonErrors.feedback: Muscle produces no carbon dioxide without oxygen. March 2026 examiners reported carbon dioxide being written where energy belonged.
Alcohol is what yeast produces. Mammalian muscle produces lactic acid — Summer 2023 examiners reported this swap.

context.setting: A baker explaining why dough rises

figures.alt: Three word equations: aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration in mammalian muscle and anaerobic respiration in yeast, with one product left blank in the first and the third.

parts.stem:
Complete this word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast.

glucose  →  energy + ______ + ______

scheme.for: alcohol
carbon dioxide

hints: Yeast makes two products besides energy, and one of them is a gas.

commonErrors.feedback: Lactic acid is the muscle product. Yeast makes alcohol and carbon dioxide.

parts.stem: Name the product of yeast respiration that makes bread dough rise.

scheme.for: carbon dioxide

hints: Which of the two products is a gas?
parts.workedSolution: Carbon dioxide — the gas forms bubbles in the dough and pushes it up.

commonErrors.feedback: Alcohol is a liquid and stays in the dough until baking drives it off. The gas that makes the dough rise is carbon dioxide.

context.setting: A hockey player sprinting at the end of a match

parts.stem: Give one similarity between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

scheme.for: both use glucose / both release energy

hints: What do all three equations have on the left?
parts.workedSolution: Both use glucose, and both release energy.

parts.stem: Give two differences between aerobic respiration and anaerobic respiration in muscle.

accepted: aerobic needs oxygen and anaerobic does not; aerobic releases much more energy and makes carbon dioxide and water while anaerobic makes lactic acid

scheme.for: any two from: aerobic needs oxygen, anaerobic does not / aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water, anaerobic in muscle produces lactic acid / aerobic releases much more energy per glucose — [1] each
scheme.examinerNote: A difference must mention both sides; a statement about one type only is not a comparison (research 03 §7.1).

hints: Each difference needs both sides of it written down.
Three differences are available: oxygen, products, energy released.
parts.workedSolution: Aerobic respiration needs oxygen while anaerobic does not, and aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and water while anaerobic respiration in muscle produces lactic acid. Aerobic respiration also releases much more energy from the same amount of glucose.

commonErrors.feedback: Only one type has been described. A difference names both and says how they differ.

parts.stem: Explain why the hockey player's muscles respire anaerobically during a sprint.

accepted: the muscles need energy faster than oxygen can be delivered, so they respire without it

scheme.for: the muscles are using energy very quickly
oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough by the lungs and blood, so respiration continues without it

hints: Two ideas: what the muscle needs, and what it cannot get quickly enough.
parts.workedSolution: Sprinting uses energy very quickly. The lungs and blood cannot deliver oxygen to the muscles fast enough to keep up, so the muscles respire anaerobically to release energy without it.

context.setting: Yeast and glucose in a boiling tube under oil

figures.alt: A boiling tube of yeast and glucose solution under a layer of oil, with a delivery tube leading into limewater.

parts.stem: Name the gas that bubbles through the limewater, and describe what the limewater does.

accepted: carbon dioxide, and the limewater turns milky

scheme.for: carbon dioxide
it turns milky

hints: The scheme's word for the limewater result is one specific adjective.
parts.workedSolution: Carbon dioxide, and the limewater turns milky.

commonErrors.feedback: 'Cloudy' is not accepted for this observation. The scheme's word is milky.

parts.stem: Explain why a layer of oil is poured on top of the yeast mixture.

accepted: the oil keeps air out so no oxygen reaches the yeast and it respires anaerobically

scheme.for: the oil stops air (oxygen) reaching the mixture
so the yeast respires anaerobically, which is what the investigation is about

hints: What is the one condition the investigation has to guarantee?
parts.workedSolution: The oil forms a barrier that keeps air, and so oxygen, away from the mixture. That makes sure the yeast respires anaerobically rather than aerobically, which is what the investigation is testing.

commonErrors.feedback: The oil is not there for warmth or evaporation. It excludes oxygen so the respiration is anaerobic.

parts.stem:
A second tube held boiled yeast and glucose solution. It produced 0 bubbles.
Explain why this tube was set up.

accepted: it is a control showing the gas in the first tube came from living yeast

scheme.for: it is a control
boiled yeast is dead and cannot respire, so it shows the gas in the first tube came from living yeast

hints: A control differs in exactly one way from the tube it is compared with.
parts.workedSolution: The boiled yeast is dead and cannot respire, so this tube is a control: it is identical to the first in every other way, and producing 0 bubbles shows that the carbon dioxide in the first tube came from living yeast.

commonErrors.feedback: Repeating gives reliability. A control shows what caused the result, and that is what this tube does.

context.setting: Three tubes of yeast counted for bubbles

parts.stem:
Use the table to calculate how many bubbles tube A would produce in 5 minutes.
Show your working out.
hints: Bubbles per minute multiplied by the number of minutes.

commonErrors.feedback: Dividing gives 4.8, which would be the rate if 24 were a total. Here 24 is already a rate, so multiply by the time.

parts.stem: Use the table to explain what tube C shows.

accepted: without glucose the yeast produces almost no carbon dioxide, so it needs a food supply to respire

scheme.for: tube C had live yeast but no glucose and gave only 1 bubble per minute
so the yeast needs glucose as a food supply before it can respire

hints: Compare tube C with tube A and name the one thing that is different.
parts.workedSolution: Tube C contained living yeast but water instead of glucose solution, and gave only 1 bubble per minute compared with 24 in tube A. Yeast therefore needs glucose as a food supply in order to respire.

questions.solutionProgram: A rate 24 bubbles/min; total in 5 min = 24 * 5 = 120; B = 0; C = 1

context.setting: A brewery and a bakery using the same organism for different reasons

parts.stem:
A brewery and a bakery both use yeast respiring without oxygen, but each wants a different product.
Suggest which product each one wants, and give a reason.

accepted: the brewery wants the alcohol and the bakery wants the carbon dioxide, which makes the dough rise

scheme.for: the brewery wants the alcohol
the bakery wants the carbon dioxide, because the gas makes the dough rise

hints: Yeast makes two products besides energy. Which is a gas, and which would you drink?
parts.workedSolution: The brewery wants the alcohol, which stays in the liquid. The bakery wants the carbon dioxide, because bubbles of the gas trapped in the dough make it rise.

context.setting: A student comparing her own muscles with a tube of yeast in the same lesson

parts.stem:
Complete the two word equations.

In mammalian muscle:  glucose  →  ______ + ______
In yeast:  glucose  →  energy + ______ + ______

scheme.for: (muscle) energy
(muscle) lactic acid
(yeast) alcohol
(yeast) carbon dioxide

hints: Four boxes, four marks. Two products for muscle, three for yeast.
Energy appears in both, because respiration always releases it.
parts.workedSolution: In mammalian muscle: glucose → energy + lactic acid. In yeast: glucose → energy + alcohol + carbon dioxide.

commonErrors.feedback: Carbon dioxide has been put into the muscle equation. Muscle produces lactic acid only; carbon dioxide belongs to yeast and to aerobic respiration.

parts.stem: Give one similarity and one difference between the two reactions in part (a).

accepted: both use glucose and release energy without oxygen; muscle produces lactic acid while yeast produces alcohol and carbon dioxide

scheme.for: similarity: both use glucose / both release energy / neither uses oxygen
difference: muscle produces lactic acid whereas yeast produces alcohol and carbon dioxide
scheme.examinerNote: A difference must name both sides.

hints: One line about what they share, one about what separates them.
parts.workedSolution: Both use glucose and release energy without needing oxygen. The difference is in the products: muscle makes lactic acid, while yeast makes alcohol and carbon dioxide.

parts.stem: Explain why a sprinter cannot keep running at full speed for very long, using ideas about anaerobic respiration.

accepted: anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose and lactic acid builds up in the muscles, causing fatigue

scheme.for: anaerobic respiration releases much less energy from each glucose molecule than aerobic respiration
lactic acid is produced
and it builds up in the muscles, which makes them tire

hints: Two problems: how much energy the route gives, and what it leaves behind.
Name the substance — 'waste' is not enough.
parts.workedSolution: Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy from each glucose molecule than aerobic respiration, so the muscles cannot keep up the same power for long. It also produces lactic acid, which builds up in the muscles and makes them tire.

commonErrors.feedback: Anaerobic respiration releases much LESS energy per glucose than aerobic respiration. That is why it cannot sustain a sprint.

context.setting: A student asked to show that yeast respires without oxygen

parts.stem:
A student is given dried yeast, glucose solution, cooking oil, limewater and the usual laboratory apparatus.
Describe how she could show that yeast respires without oxygen, and what results she would expect.
Your written communication is assessed in this question, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; organised clearly; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: mix the yeast with glucose solution in a boiling tube
cover the mixture with a layer of oil to keep air out
close the tube with a bung and a delivery tube leading into limewater
keep the tube warm, for example in a water bath at about 30 °C
bubbles of gas pass into the limewater and it turns milky, showing carbon dioxide
set up a control with boiled yeast, which produces no bubbles
the other product, alcohol, stays in the liquid; the results show yeast respires anaerobically

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Two things are easy to leave out: the oil, and the control with boiled yeast.
Say what the limewater does as well as that you use it — the observation is an indicative point of its own.
parts.workedSolution: Mix the dried yeast with glucose solution in a boiling tube and pour a layer of cooking oil on top so that air, and therefore oxygen, cannot reach the mixture. Close the tube with a bung carrying a delivery tube that leads into a second tube of limewater, and stand the apparatus in a water bath at about 30 °C to keep it warm. Bubbles of gas pass into the limewater and it turns milky, which shows that carbon dioxide is being produced. Set up an identical tube containing boiled yeast as a control: it produces no bubbles, showing the gas came from living yeast. The yeast's other product, alcohol, stays in the liquid. Together these results show that yeast respires without oxygen.

commonErrors.feedback: The oil layer is missing, and without it oxygen reaches the yeast so the respiration would not be anaerobic. It is one of the seven indicative points.

findTheMistake.stem:
Pádraig is asked: 'Complete this word equation for anaerobic respiration in a mammalian muscle: glucose → ______ + ______ [2]'
His answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lactic acid is right, so half the answer is there. The other box needs **energy**, not carbon dioxide. A muscle respiring without oxygen makes no carbon dioxide at all — that gas comes from the aerobic route and from yeast.
findTheMistake.feedback: One of the two marks: lactic acid is correct and specific. The lost mark is a habit worth fixing, because March 2026's examiners saw it across the cohort — candidates completed the equation with lactic acid and then reached for carbon dioxide to fill the second box. Every respiration equation on this specification has energy among its products, so write energy in first and then ask what else the route makes.

prompts.prompt: For a mammalian muscle, write the word equation for anaerobic respiration.
Write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast.
Which anaerobic product belongs to muscle and which to yeast?
prompts.answer: Lactic acid is muscle. Alcohol and carbon dioxide are yeast. Muscle produces no gas at all.

prompts.prompt: Give one similarity and one difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
prompts.answer: Both use glucose and release energy. Aerobic needs oxygen and releases much more energy per glucose; anaerobic needs none and releases much less.

prompts.prompt: How do you show that yeast is respiring, and what is the oil for?
prompts.answer: Bubble the gas through limewater: it turns milky, showing carbon dioxide. The oil layer keeps air out so the respiration is anaerobic.
